text: Then the cavalry arrives: a Gate Rescue van through the enclosure gate, police cars behind it.
Choi jumps down with a megaphone and Kanghan's worst nightmare: paperwork. The gate is legally his.
The Kanghan guards look at each other, and lower their batons.
Yerin sprints across the mud with her first-aid bag, Bomi right behind her.
Yerin's light closes his cuts but can't stop the shaking. He changes the subject. He has a call to make.
She holds the phone to his ear, his trembling fingers on her wrist.
Seoa is shouting before he can say hello. He smiles through the mud and promises dinner at seven.
Foil blankets go round, police tape off the steel plate, and the summons sit together by Borro.
Uncle Pyo grips Jaeha's shaking hand. Ten years he walked out of gates as a number. Tonight, as himself.
Moon Ahin gives Choi her phone, sure nobody can bury Kanghan's heir. Choi has seen a red lamp vanish from a report.
Alone in the van, Choi makes a copy anyway, onto a cheap USB stick.
Then he tucks the stick between two rolls of kimbap.
The perfect hiding place, he decides, having forgotten what Nib once did to his kimbap.
At dawn they sit in a row of foil blankets as the sun rises over the Han. Jaeha counts them again.
Moon Ahin was raised never to name a husk, in case she lost it. Now she asks him how you'd even start. His advice: look properly.
Her lead husk stands alone against the sunrise. Saebyeok, she calls him. It means dawn.
Nine a.m., the Association. Choi hands the evidence to Inspector Ryu, and holds on a second too long.
Then Deputy Director Hwang steps between them, smiling, and takes charge of it personally.
Ryu lets go of the bag. He doesn't look happy about it.
At four, everyone crowds into the Gate Rescue break room for the Association's press conference.
Hwang buries it with a sorrowful smile: the video might be staged, and day labourers can't be trusted.
Ho throws his cup at the wall. Pyo doesn't move. Last night he walked out a person. On the news, he's unreliable.
Jaeha's eyes narrow at the screen.
As Hwang turns away, his lapel flips over, and underneath is a small silver hexagon pin.
Bomi freezes the frame: Kanghan's mark, the one on every tank in the pit. Choi isn't even surprised.
Bomi is on her feet. A million subscribers, and she'd like to see Kanghan bury that.
Jaeha shakes his head. Post it now, and Kanghan sues Moon Ahin. Proof only gets one shot. Not yet.
Choi pats the kimbap box. The copy will keep, filed under tuna.
In the corner, Lyra hears only one word, and it's tuna.
Jaeha's coffee trembles in rings, and slops onto his knee.
Yerin watches his hands. Whatever this is, her light didn't fix it.
Earlier that afternoon, Moon Ahin strides through Kanghan Tower in a fresh white coat, hair loose, furious.
Her uncle, Director Baek Taegun, greets her with a family man's concern, as if she'd only missed curfew.
She doesn't raise her voice. She doesn't need to. Nothing with the family seal on it happens without her uncle knowing.
Baek doesn't deny it. He lists what Kanghan cores keep running in hospitals, starting with the incubators.
Then he turns that kind face on her and asks it, gently. Does she want the hospitals dark, Ahin?
She has no answer. The baton trembles at her side.
His voice stays gentle. Officially, nothing happened. The family expects her for Sunday dinner.
She walks to the door without a word.
At the door, she tells him her first husk's name. He taught her never to give them one. That's her answer.
The door clicks shut, and one eyebrow lifts behind his glasses.
Five forty, the columbarium. Jaeha walks the white corridor alone, Minseok's rusted lamp in his hand.
He sets the lamp on the ledge beside Choi's can of coffee, his hands trembling.
Hands in his pocket, he reports to the photo like a trap-tester after a job: the door, the giant, the promise.
Behind the glass, Minseok grins, thumb up.
He checks the time, both hands steadying the phone. Dinner is at seven, and he's famous for being late.
At dusk, Han Sora lounges in a sports car on an overpass, wrist bandaged. Her phone buzzes.
It's the Director. She confesses to losing his compass before he can ask, not sounding sorry at all.
Baek stands at his window as the city lights up. He isn't angry. He's curious.
So she tells him. The Operator out-thought her compass, and his archer chose to miss her. She's still delighted.
Baek has one question, and it isn't about the compass. Did the Operator kill anyone?
For once, Sora is serious. Nobody died, and he bled for the competition's husks. Now it's catching up with him. His hands are going.
Baek's gloved hand tightens on the cane's glowing core.
Her smile creeps back. A man who can't hold chopsticks would be easy to collect.
Behind his glasses, Baek's eyes don't move. He's weighing something.
No. Baek forbids it. Nobody lays a finger on the Operator.
Sora frowns. For once, she can't read the plan.
And for the first time, Baek's polite smile reaches its full width. Make him come to us.
Across the city, warm bulbs light a small rooftop in Mangwon. A figure in a hoodie hurries up the stairs, for once not late.
